The biggest source of the gases that trigger photochemical smog is the automobile. In the Bay Area, about 61% of the reactive organic gases and 46% of the nitrogen oxides come from cars and light duty trucks. After peaking in 1965, Bay Area oxidant levels have shown a clear downward trend for the past 11 years, despite large annual weather-induced fluctuations. Days exceeding the Federal one-hour standard of .08 ppm averaged 131 in the 1965-69 pentad and 85 in the 1970-74 pentad. For the 1975 base year, there were 69 days over standard, and preliminary totals for 1976 show 65 days.
In the Bay Area, high oxidant levels have exhibited a migration to the southeast in recent years. San Leandro led (with over .15 ppm) in 1964 and 1965; Livermore led (with over .14 ppm) in 1968 and 1960; San Jose led (with .11 to .13 ppm) in 1974 and 1975. These highest station averages have fortunately decreased at nearly the same rate as the over-all District average. The reasons for the shift appear quite complex-related to the 15-year shifts in population and vehicle use, and to the changes in emission mix and emission patterns. Additionally, the increases in emissions of primary contaminants have been into the sheltered valleys topographically and meteorologically least favorable for mixing and dispersion. Thus, Since the oxidant levels experienced in the Bay Area in recent years reached 2-3 times the standard, this area has been designated by EPA as a non-attainment area for oxides.
Comment:
The final statement needs to explain what the two numbers represent under Average Daily Traffic.
Response:
The two numbers represent the average duty traffic at the intersection of the listed streets. By way of example, on page 35, Bird Avenue is shown. Bird Avenue is a north/south arterial and it intersects with West Virginia Avenue and Willow Street. The 13930 ADT would be for southbound traffic at West Virginia; the 6450 ADT would be for southbound traffic at Willow Street. Another way of showing this:
